paras: The lynching of Levi Smith was the hanging of a young man from Crawford County, Indiana, by a mob near Buleyville, Harrison County, Kentucky, in late August 1881. Smith was accused of killing a man and fleeing, and the mob pursued and hanged him. Indiana sources presented him as a "desperado" with a record of violence, and the story ran mainly as a brief item in Midwestern crime roundups.

Smith's parents lived at Leavenworth, Indiana, and a dispatch from that town described them as "very respectable people." The same dispatch said he "had committed several murders and narrowly escaped each time." The Richmond Palladium gave a narrower account of his past, saying he had been in three cutting affrays in Crawford and Harrison counties and had "barely slipped through" the law.

According to the National Associated Press report, Smith killed a man and fled, and a Kentucky mob pursued him and hanged him near Buleyville. The Palladium said instead that he was hanged at Buleyville for murdering a man with whom he had quarreled. Neither account names the man Smith was accused of killing, the members of the mob, or the date, hour, and exact site of the hanging, beyond a dispatch dated August 31. No report gives the race of Smith or of the man he was said to have killed.
The coverage contains no report of an inquest, arrests, or any official response to the hanging.

The story first appeared on September 1, 1881, in the Omaha Daily Bee under the headline "Young Desperado Lynched" and in the "State News" column of the Richmond Daily Palladium. Both reports came from Indiana and took the mob's justification at face value, describing Smith as a "young desperado" or as "one of the worst men Crawford county ever produced." A week later a one-sentence version ran among the shootings and murders of the syndicated "Tragical Tales" column in the Mower County Transcript of Minnesota and the Watertown Republican of Wisconsin, and on September 10 in the Superior Times. No Kentucky paper's report and no editorial comment on the mob appear in the coverage.

bases: Both independent reports say a mob hanged Levi Smith after he was accused of killing a man (A1, A2).
A 'mob' pursued and hanged Smith without any legal process, as punishment for a killing he was accused of (A1, A2); the mob's size is not given, but the papers call it a mob.

The National Associated Press dispatch (A1) and the differently worded Indiana state-news item (A2) agree on the hanging by a mob at or near Buleyville, Ky.; both come from Indiana sources, and no Kentucky report was found.

Midwestern weeklies ran a one-sentence version in the syndicated 'Tragical Tales' crime roundup.
